extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of poetry and literary criticism (educated public, translators, poets)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for writing, translating, and evaluating poetry (especially love-lyrics and epic poetry), including expectations about faithfulness in translation, suitability of diction/ornament, and structural/affective aims for heroic poems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments must grow out of the occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Sentiment must grow out of the Occasion, and be suitable to the Circumstances of the Character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid witty turns or quaintnesses that are merely display; when a humble servant speaks fine things, those lines should express genuine feeling appropriate to his station, not showmanship. 'Where this Rule is transgressed ... is but shewing his Mistress how well he can dress, instead of saying how well he loves.' Lace and drapery (ornamental verbal dressing) should not substitute for real passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish genuine passion from artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of true Taste can distinguish the exertion of a mind which overflows with tender sentiments from the labour of one which is only describing distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should avoid affected 'quaintnesses and Turns of Imagination' that signal contrivance; aim for language and imagery that feel spontaneous and emergent from the emotion rather than self-consciously clever.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translations should preserve sentiment and adapt form
rubrics_metrics.description: A faithful translation keeps to the Sentiments 'without adding or diminishing' while adapting metrics and measures to suit the target tongue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The translator may 'bind it in stricter Measures, as being more proper for our Tongue,' but must retain the original spirit; accept that original loose or unequal numbers might better suit the source language's genius, yet adjust form for readability and poetic propriety in the target language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting theological or expository aims override poetic craft
rubrics_metrics.description: An author who becomes 'so attentive to his Divinity, that he has neglected his Poetry' weakens the poem where narration becomes doctrinal exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain poetic qualities—imagery, rhythm, and imaginative presence—even when the subject requires theological or philosophical material; do not sacrifice poetic expression for didactic argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer vivid, visual presentation (show) over abstract narration (tell)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting scenes in vision (vivid, pictorial description) is preferable to dry narration; splitting a work into visible parts and written narrative can feel uneven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic likens mixing vision and narration to a history-painter putting color on half a subject and writing the rest; where possible, render episodes in lively, visible detail rather than summarizing them in narrative prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: An heroic/epic poem ought to end happily (consolatory closure)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Heroick Poem, according to the best Critics, ought to end happily, leaving the reader, after many doubts and sorrows, in a state of tranquility and satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject resists a naturally happy ending, the poet should devise methods to supply consolatory closure (e.g., showing the adversary humbled and the protagonists comforted by visions/promises) so the reader's emotional arc resolves peacefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and ornament episodes suited to poetic treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the subject is capable of poetical ornaments (examples: the Confusion at Babel, the Plagues of Egypt, a storm of hail and fire), these portions should be treated with strong, vivid imagery and elevated diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify episodes apt for sublime or pictorial treatment and invest them with concentrated poetic power; such scenes can raise the poem and supply striking, memorable passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground literary taste by comparing texts with real places and history
rubrics_metrics.description: Improving one's taste in ancient authors is aided by 'seeing the Places where they lived' and comparing the country’s natural face with the descriptions they gave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use real-world observation—visiting celebrated sites, examining local particulars—to enrich understanding of classical descriptions and to draw moral or imaginative conclusions (e.g., reflections on time, ruins, and the uncertainty of human things).
